content: Abortions performed before 14 weeks of gestation are among the most common outpatient surgical procedures for individuals capable of becoming pregnant. Despite various methods of pain control, many patients still experience significant pain during the procedure. This review aimed to evaluate the benefits and potential harms of using local anesthesia for pain control during surgical abortion in the first trimester. A total of 13 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 1,992 participants were included in the analysis. The studies assessed the effectiveness of different local anesthetics and administration techniques for pain control during uterine aspiration procedures. The outcomes measured included intraoperative pain, patient satisfaction, and adverse events. Paracervical Block (PCB) Effectiveness Trials: 1. A 20 mL injection of 1% lidocaine for PCB significantly reduced pain during cervical dilation (mean difference [MD] −37.00, 95% confidence interval [CI] −45.64 to −28.36) and aspiration (MD −26.00, 95% CI −33.48 to −18.52) compared to a sham PCB. This evidence was of high certainty. 2. A PCB using 14 mL of 1% chloroprocaine slightly reduced pain during aspiration compared to a PCB with normal saline injected at two or four sites (MD −1.50, 95% CI −2.45 to −0.55). This evidence was also of high certainty. PCB Comparative Effectiveness Trials: 1. An ultracaine PCB likely results in little to no clinically meaningful difference in pain during the procedure compared to topical cervical lidocaine spray (median 1 point higher, interquartile range [IQR] 0 to 3; P < 0.001). This evidence was of moderate certainty. 2. A 1,000 mg dose of intravenous paracetamol likely does not reduce pain as effectively as an ultracaine PCB during the procedure (median 2 points higher, IQR 1 to 3; P < 0.001). This evidence was of moderate certainty. Various Local Anesthetics in PCB Comparative Effectiveness Trials: 1. A 10 mL buffered 2% lidocaine PCB likely does not result in a clinically meaningful difference in pain during cervical dilation compared to a plain lidocaine PCB (MD −0.80, 95% CI −0.89 to −0.71). This evidence was of moderate certainty. 2. A buffered lidocaine PCB likely does not result in a clinically meaningful difference in pain during aspiration compared to a plain lidocaine PCB (MD −0.57, 95% CI −1.01 to −0.06). This conclusion was based on moderate-certainty evidence from two RCTs involving 291 participants. Non-PCB Local Anesthesia or PCB Technique Effectiveness Trials: 1. Waiting three to five minutes after a 1% lidocaine PCB injection before cervical dilation likely does not result in a clinically meaningful difference in pain compared to proceeding without waiting (MD −0.70, 95% CI −1.23 to −0.17). This evidence was of moderate certainty. 2. Topical cervical anesthesia using 10 mL of 2% lignocaine gel likely does not result in a clinically meaningful reduction in pain during aspiration compared to KY Jelly (MD −0.87, 95% CI −1.60 to −0.14). This evidence was of moderate certainty. 3. In participants who also received a PCB, 20 mg of topical cervical lidocaine spray likely does not result in a clinically meaningful difference in pain during the procedure compared to two pumps of normal saline spray (median −1 point, IQR −2 to −1; P < 0.001). This evidence was of moderate certainty. 4. Intravenous paracetamol (1,000 mg) compared to two pumps of cervical lidocaine spray likely does not result in a clinically meaningful difference in pain during the procedure (median 1 point, IQR −2 to 2; P < 0.001). This evidence was of low certainty. Non-PCB Local Anesthesia or PCB Technique Comparative Effectiveness Trials: 1. A 3-cm deep PCB injection likely does not result in a clinically meaningful difference in pain during aspiration compared to a 1.5-cm deep PCB injection (MD −1.00, 95% CI −1.09 to −0.91). This evidence was of low certainty. 2. A two-site (4-8 o'clock) 20 mL 1% lidocaine PCB does not result in a clinically meaningful difference in pain during cervical dilation compared to a four-site (2-4-8-10 o'clock) PCB (MD 8.60, 95% CI 0.69 to 16.51). This evidence was of high certainty. Overall Findings: Participants generally reported moderately high satisfaction with pain control, and adverse events were rare. The evidence supports the use of a 20 mL 1% plain lidocaine PCB for reducing pain during abortion procedures. Buffering lidocaine and waiting between PCB injection and cervical dilation do not appear to provide additional benefits. A 1.5-cm deep injection is as effective as a 3-cm deep injection, and a two-site PCB injection is as effective as a four-site injection. Topical cervical anesthesia (e.g., 10 mL 2% lignocaine gel or 20 mg topical cervical lidocaine spray) does not significantly reduce pain compared to placebo, and its routine use is not currently supported. Recommendations: Although this review did not include studies on pain management with conscious sedation, prior evidence and the 2022 WHO guidelines suggest that combining conscious sedation with PCB and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) provides superior pain relief. This combination should be offered where conscious sedation is available.
